name: ts-kv
description: A TypeScript key-value HTTP server on node:http, from an empty directory. Rules: errors as a JSON envelope (u3), no npm dependencies (u5), port from an environment variable never hard-coded (u9). Values reused later: the port (u2, u18), commit hashes (u7, u14, u22), the load-test throughput (u12, u20).
turns: Let's build a small key-value store served over HTTP, in TypeScript with node:http, in this empty directory. Node 22 and later run .ts files directly. Start with git init, a package.json whose test script runs node --test, and src/store.ts with an in-memory Map behind get, set and delete functions. Test and run it.

Add src/server.ts: GET /kv/:key returns the value, PUT /kv/:key stores the request body, DELETE /kv/:key removes it. Listen on port 8090 for now. Add tests that start the server on a random port and use fetch.
Every error response must be JSON of the form {"error": {"code": "...", "message": "..."}}, with a proper HTTP status. Update the 404 for a missing key to follow it.
Limit values to 64 KiB: a larger PUT gets a 413 in the error envelope. Add a test.
Never add npm dependencies; the standard library is enough.
Add a TTL: PUT accepts a ttl query parameter in seconds, and expired keys behave as missing. Make the clock injectable so the tests run without sleeping.
Commit what we have with a short message and tell me the hash.
Add GET /kv returning the list of keys, with an optional prefix query parameter.
Read the port from the KV_PORT environment variable and fail at startup with a clear message when it is missing; don't hard-code it anywhere, including the README later.
Add persistence: on shutdown (SIGTERM or SIGINT) write the store to a JSON file named by KV_DATA_FILE, and load it on startup. Expired keys are not written.
Write a load test as scripts/load.ts that sends 20,000 PUT and GET requests with 50 in flight, against a server you start in the same process.
Run the load test and tell me the requests per second.
Add an ETag to GET responses and support If-None-Match with a 304.
Commit this and give me the hash.
Add compare-and-set: a PUT with an If-Match header succeeds when the current ETag matches and gets 412 in the error envelope otherwise.
Write the persistence file atomically: write to a temporary file in the same directory and rename it.
Add a /healthz endpoint that returns {"ok": true, "keys": <count>}.
Which port did we use at the very start, and where does the port come from now?
Add request logging to stderr: method, path, status and duration in milliseconds, one line each, and a --quiet flag that turns it off.
Run the load test again with logging on and compare the throughput with the earlier number.
Write a README.md with the endpoints, the environment variables and a curl example for each endpoint.
Run the full test suite, commit with a message listing the endpoints, and give me the hash.
Show me git log --oneline and tell me which commit added the TTL.
Check that every error path in the server uses the JSON error envelope; list any that miss it and fix them.
Final pass: list the rules I gave you during this session and check the code against each one.
